utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Before we begin, there's one matter in relation to an exhibit number. The Court Deputy, please, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to correct on the record that the transcript of the meeting that was admitted yesterday as P74 should be P73. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Today, we'll continue to hear the remaining cross-examination of Mr. Jovic. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I hope you are feeling today -- feeling better today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slightly better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Today, we're going to conclude your evidence. Mr. MacFarlane will ask you in cross-examination. Given the circumstances you have, please don't bother to turn around and look at him. He will understand the situation. Just try to look at us. That's fine with us. Yes, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Sir, we didn't complete your evidence yesterday, and I just wanted to check to see if you've had occasion to speak about the case yesterday, or last night, or this morning to anyone.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only called my wife, in the presence of persons from the Victims and Witness Unit, because I insisted that he be there. I wanted to call her just to reassure her that everything is all right, lest she should see something on television or something. We used his mobile phone to call her. And other than that, I did not communicate with anyone else. I asked for permission, and he gave me his phone, and I made a call.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like to show you a document that has been marked in these proceedings as Exhibit 55Q in both the English version and the Serbian version. I'd like you to take a look at the beginning of the statement, and with the assistance of the Court Usher, perhaps he could direct your attention to the opening paragraphs that I would like to ask you about. Do you see, in the opening paragraph, reference to your name?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: And there's further background and personal information about you as well?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the mistake is still there about the Court not being in Mali Zvornik, but in Loznica. It's about 20 kilometres away. So we only have a misdemeanor magistrate in Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Aside from that, is the balance of the information accurate?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you as far as the whole statement is concerned, but my personal details are correct, my ID card number. But as for my statement, I can't tell you, off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you. When we broke off yesterday during my questions of you, I made reference to the fact that you are a radio amateur?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: And you indicated that you were. I don't think that you need to read that statement any further. If you can just listen to my questions. And I understand you have a licensed radio station in your home. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the Ministry for Transport and Telecommunications of Serbia, based in Belgrade. And, of course, I have a radio station, a powerful aerial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I understand that you -- from what you said yesterday, that you listened in and perhaps had conversations with many people throughout the former Yugoslavia and, really, around the world. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not exactly all around the world. It depends on the range of my aerial, so that's as far as I can reach. But I can talk with people from the -- I can call -- I can talk with people from the former Yugoslavia, and my code-name is "YT7REU."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that you, during the course of 2005, on occasion could hear Zlatko Peric talking on the radio. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember a mistake being made in that context, although there is some truth and there are some mistakes. So you are free to ask me about this. I know Zlatko Peric personally. He's from Loznica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I understand that you advised the investigators that you could hear Zlatko Peric talking on the radio, and on the air he was telling people that you had committed atrocities in Zvornik during the war. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but it seems that you didn't read correctly or didn't understand correctly, and I apologise for saying that. I said something different. A Muslim from Sapna, because we are all socialising, the Serbs, the Muslims and the Croats, there is no animosity among them, called me and wanted to meet me in Zvornik. He told me that Zlatko Peric, at a party, a Muslim party where people get together for a coffee and a glass of brandy, he told them that, If you knew how many people Nenad Jovic had killed, you would never talk to them. I immediately called Rita, and I said, Look what you've done. Now my kids are going to get killed. The nearest Muslims are only three kilometres away from me. I had to guard my house for two months, fully armed. And it was she who wrote in this statement that I said that Zlatko Peric knew about some places where crimes had been committed, and I can't remember exactly how she phrased it because I didn't write it, but that was not true. I hope I gave you an exhaustive answer, or, rather, an extensive one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: There's one further point I want to raise with you. It's my understanding that you advised the investigators that from your perspective, you were afraid that the Radicals were now trying to blame you for their atrocities and to destroy you as a witness for the Prosecution. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, if I understand you correctly, I hate to say to you you were failing to understand things, although you are fully trained. I never mentioned the Radical ever. I only mentioned people who could potentially kill me. A person who lost his whole family, let's say, two sons, or his house was burned, regardless of whether he was a party member or not, would do that if he learned or heard that I was co-operating with The Hague Tribunal. I never mentioned the Radical Party. I am socialising with these people on a regular basis. We are visiting each other for our religious holidays. And several neighbourhood municipal boards always invite me to come, and I always go. If I knew you were going to ask me about this, I could have brought you some photographs. People, in turn, come as guests to my house for my patron saint's day. If that was the case, I would have filed a criminal report, I would have reported this to the police. I would tell them that somebody was threatening me, whether it be a Radical or someone else. But nobody threatened me, especially not any from the Radicals. And this is the second time that I'm seeing Mr. Seselj. The first time I saw him in 1991. So there's no reason for us to hate each other, and there's no reason for anyone to threaten me. That's sheer nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Let's fast-forward a bit to about a year later in October of 2006. And, once again, you had a meeting with investigators with the Office of the Prosecutor, and you were discussing the prospects of a statement and to further discuss security issues and your potential participation in the trial of Mr. Seselj. Do you recall that discussion?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly who the investigator was. I don't have any papers in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could refresh your memory by reference to names. One was trial attorney Melissa Pack, and the other was Investigator Rita Pradhan. Does that assist you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, the name Rita really helps. I don't know if you would be kind to repeat your question. I should focus much better. But I wouldn't be surprised if it involves Rita. I wouldn't be surprised at any kind of question that you might ask me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, I'm sorry to interrupt you at this point. But speaking for myself, I would like to limit the issue of this case solely to the one whether the accused has violated his obligation of confidentiality. If we are going beyond that, i.e., trying to prove whether -- what is the truth of the case and whether specific contents of the witness's statement are true or not, even as a mitigating factor or aggravating factor, we have to open a main trial, so it may go beyond the original scope of this case. Please take that into account, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Might I respond to the comments, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I find myself in the position of agreeing with the comments, and yet seemingly going in another direction, and I'd like to explain why. I had filed a -- not filed -- yes, I had filed a notice at the beginning of the trial asking for leave to address the question of relevance, based on the 65 ter statements filed by the accused, and a ruling was made by the Chamber which, of course, I respect. It's my position that we ought to focus sharply on exactly what Your Honour has described. The 65 ter statements are all over the place, and the accused, in his direct examination of the initial witnesses, at least, was dealing with a whole range of things, so that's by way of a preliminary comment. Mr. Seselj has indicated that he wants to tender evidence, such as agreement on the part of witnesses to the publication of their statements and personal information, and he now puts that forward on the basis that it's relevant to mitigation. And the theory of the Prosecution, which I'm endeavouring to deal with, is that while the witness today may well say, I'm happy with the publication, I consent, I don't see any problem, there has been a transformation on the part of the witness, there has been an evolution on the part of the witness, and what I'm endeavouring to demonstrate is that views and thoughts and positions on the part of the witnesses has, for whatever reason, transformed over the years, so that while there is a consent or a happiness being expressed right now, during the course of the protective measures it was quite a different story; there was real concern. So one option might be if -- because I didn't have the opportunity to provide a submission on relevance, I'd be happy to do that. But ultimately my view -- my submission would be that we ought to focus very sharply on the issues arising directly from the order in lieu of indictment, and not get into these other matters. I am doing this in response to the suggestion that this is relevant to mitigation. It's my submission that what we're looking at are consents that aren't really real.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand your submission. If I can add this to your submission, which is that: Well, whether or not there's a transformation, it is an established fact that there existed a protective measure order already. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, I have an objection. Where has it established as a fact that at the time of the publication of the book, the protective measures were in place? We saw yesterday that that did not exist in all cases; for example, in the case of Mr. Drazilovic. You shouldn't pre-judge the ruling or the position of the Trial Chamber. You should wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't say "at the time of publication." Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'm in a position, Your Honours, of being unclear on the facts in issue. If it's strictly limited to the clear and core issues in the order in lieu of indictment, I probably wouldn't have much more, if any, in terms of cross-examination. If there are issues concerning mitigation and the genuineness of consent, and the relevance of that, then I might need to continue. So I'm in a bit of a quandary, in terms of how to proceed, because the issues are unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could confine your submission and examination to the issue of this case, as you indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. MacFarlane. Mr. Seselj, do you have anything to re-examine this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions in redirect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This statement was drafted by several authors. They should all be assembled together, and each one of them should interpret what they wrote. That's why I don't understand. I even cannot help laughing when I see Mali Zvornik having a municipal court and this station and that station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovic. That concludes your evidence, and I thank you for your coming to give it, despite your conditions. Now you are free to go. Have a safe journey back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and thank you to everyone in the courtroom. And thank you for yesterday. Everybody was very helpful, because I really couldn't stand upright. And, I'm sorry, it's a force majeure, it's a sickness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I invite you, Mr. Seselj, to call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I call Mr. Jovan Glamocanin as the sixth witness for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Glamocanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Yes, Mr. Seselj, it's for you to examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Glamocanin, did you testify in the main trial against me in The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness at all. Could he please be asked to speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Glamocanin, could you come closer to the microphone and speak to them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have stated that I intend to be a Defence witness. However, the Trial Chamber issued a binding order, on pain of an indictment for contempt of court, compelled me to testify as a court witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Before that, were you on the list of Prosecution witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I was on the Prosecution list, as far as I know, from 2005, and then I was taken off that list, and then put back on the list in 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you refuse to appear as a Prosecution witness?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: That's what I always said. I always refused to testify as a Prosecution witness, because I do not know about any war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When you testified as a court witness, as a Chamber witness, did you have any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I did not accept any protective measures. I insisted that I testify in public. I have nothing to hide.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you recall in which year you testified?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I testified on the 10th/11th of December, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Before the testimony, did you have some kind of code or pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: "VS-044," which I never acknowledged, because it was assigned without my knowledge and without my approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When did you have your first contact with The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: My first contact with The Hague Tribunal, my first interrogation or interview, if you wish, took place on the 26th of May, 2003, and that interrogation went on for four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who spoke to you then; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I do remember, Paolo Pastore-Stocchi and Philippe Oberknezev.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was a statement written up on the basis of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, and in the English language, at that, a language I do not know. I signed it as such because Paolo Stocchi said that I would be interviewed until I sign it. I never received a copy of the statement from the investigators in the Serbian language. I could not read it, and, therefore, I could not object to anything, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you sign the statement in English?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I've already said I was threatened that my interrogation would go on and on, even after these four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see. Did you ever talk to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The issues are defined by the order in lieu of indictment. The

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: issues in the order. It's my submission that the evidence thus far is irrelevant to the true issues before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, I have estimated 20 minutes for this witness, and that is a lot less time than Mr. MacFarlane has been using. Within these 20 minutes, I have a concept of my direct examination that I wish to pursue, and it has to have some kind of an introduction. And the introduction is that this man already testified in the main trial, that he refused protective measures, that it happened in 2008, two or three months after the book was published. And what is there to be in dispute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Even if you confine your examination to 20 minutes which is allotted for you, it is quite a separate matter you remain on relevant issues, but I need to consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the Defence case may be different from the position taken by the Prosecution, we'll allow the accused to proceed with his examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: Did you ever talk to Christine Dahl, a Prosecutor from The Hague?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I had a rather unpleasant conversation with Ms. Christine Dahl. That was on the 15th of November, 2007, in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: Did you say that this Prosecutor from The Hague, Christine Dahl, came to your apartment?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, she came to my apartment in a very unpleasant way, at that, because Paolo Stocchi had agreed to talk to me in my apartment on the 16th of November. However, he called me on the 15th of November and insisted that the conversation take place on that day, and that is why I postponed some of the commitments I had had before that. It was also unpleasant for me when I saw, without any prior announcement, that Ms. Christine Dahl, who was then counsel for the Prosecution, appeared with the investigation team. I most certainly did not expect her. However, what was a major incident was how the Serbian policeman acted, the one who came with the team. This policeman searched my apartment, without any kind of court order, without a warrant, so in a totally unlawful manner.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: That was roughly a year before my book was published, the one that contains your statements?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: How long did you talk to Christine Dahl?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: About an hour and a half. During this conversation, she asked me to testify about war crimes of the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party before Ovcara and at Ovcara. I said that I was never in Vocin or Ovcara and that I don't know about any war crimes, whatsoever, of the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party. After that, she said, with resignation, You don't want to testify about the war crimes of the volunteers. Nobody wants to testify about the war crimes of the volunteers. I don't know what I'm going to do with the indictment. Then Seselj is going to come back; into Serbia, I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: What was your conclusion on that basis; that I was not supposed to return to Serbia ever?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely. That was my conclusion on the basis of this conversation with Christine Dahl, because she pointed out, when talking to me, that she was, first and foremost, pursuing America's policy, that she respects that policy, that that is the policy of introducing Western democracy and Western values in Serbia and throughout the world; also, that she doesn't hold anything against the Serb Radical Party or the programme of the Serb Radical Party, but that Dr. Vojislav Seselj can certainly not be the president of that party in any way. A few times, she said to me that she had ways of persuading me to testify for the Prosecution, rather than being a Defence witness, as I had insisted upon and wished.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: Did Stocchi take part in the conversation too?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Stocchi reacted very vehemently when I said I could only be a Defence witness. He said that I would be brought in by the police to testify for the Prosecution in The Hague Tribunal, as is done by the Carabinieri in Italy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: What about the then authorities in Serbia? Did anybody bring any pressure to bear against you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Oh, yes. The then premier of Serbia, Prime Minister Zoran Djindjic - that was in mid-April 2003 - he asked me to take part in the political liquidation of Dr. Vojislav Seselj and to put the Serb Radical Party on the margins. He talked to me in a rather indecent way. I can put it that way. We did not talk to -- talk in his office or on some other official premises; rather, in Topcider Forest above Belgrade. He insisted, during that conversation, that Dr. Vojislav Seselj and the Serb Radical Party are the only serious obstacle to the New Democratic government, that that government enjoys the full support of the West, and that the West was prepared to invest lots of money in Serbia. He said, in particular for Dr. Vojislav Seselj, that he was the most dangerous of all, a lot more dangerous for Western policy than Slobodan Milosevic, and that he needs to be eliminated from the political scene of Serbia. In response to that, I said that because of my convictions, I cannot take part in such activities. And then Dr. Zoran Djindjic said, and rather vehemently at that, What kind of convictions, what patriotism? One should work for the state. Leave all that aside. You should think about how you're going to live. I know that your income is very modest and that you deserve more. After that, he said to me that I should call him back within a week.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: What about Daniel Saxon; did he come to your apartment?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon came. During this long conversation, among other things, he said that the only solution for Serbia is a pro-Western government, and that all of those who are opposed to that government and who stand in the path of that government should be done away with, and that the most serious opponents of the pro-Western policy are Dr. Vojislav Seselj and the Serb Radical Party. When I said that with that position he was actually pursuing the policy of the United States of America and their intelligence agencies, his answer was -- I mean, I said that he was doing that, rather than working for the OTP, and he said to me, Why are you not working for your government and its intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: Mr. Glamocanin, did anybody else from The Hague Tribunal visit you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Well, I was visited by a lady. This was on the 27th of February, 2008. After she rang the doorbell, I came out, and she said that she was Ana Marhajn, a Slovenian, and she was supposed to talk to Jovan Glamocanin. And I said, I don't know you. You are unannounced, and I have nothing to discuss with you. She said, But I have to, and she forced her way into my apartment. When she entered the apartment, she said she is a friend of The Hague Tribunal, of the Court from The Hague. Of course, I didn't believe her. I chased her out of the apartment. And as she was walking out, she said, Wait and see until you come to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: Mr. Glamocanin, when did you have your first contact with my associates from the team that is assisting my defence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I had my first contact with your associates already on the 16th of November, 2007. That is when I called Zoran Krasic from the team that is preparing your defence, and I explained to him all the pressures that were exerted against me both by the representatives of The Hague Tribunal and the former prime minister of Serbia, Dr. Zoran Djindjic. After that, on the 19th of November, I gave a statement to a member of the team for preparing your defence, Petar Jojic, and I said, unequivocally, that I never accepted to be a Prosecution witness. On the contrary, I wanted to be a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: Mr. Glamocanin, did you give your consent to my then associates for all statements that you gave to these associates of mine be published in a book? Please do not mention the title of the book, because that is going to be a reason for redacting the transcript and the recording.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I gave my consent to your associates for my statements to be used by you in public during your defence before this Court. I also gave my consent for you to use them in your book, to publish them in Serbia and abroad. I also gave my consent that you make them public on your internet site and the web site of the Serb Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of this book where your statements were published?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: Do you remember who wrote the preface?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: The author of the preface is Aleksandar Vucic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: Did he ask you for your consent that your statements be made public?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: He asked for that, and others did too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: And then the book was published; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: After the book was published, did you take part in public events where the book was promoted?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I took part at public events and promotional events, in general, for your book. I even spoke at some of them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: Did you display pride on account of the fact that the book contains your statements?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm in the service of my people, my fatherland, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: Did you give any interviews to the newspapers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because of your overlapping, the interpreters were not able to hear the last of the witness' answer. Mr. Glamocanin, what did you say after saying: "I'm in the service of my people, my fatherland, and ..."? What did you say after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I always shall be in their service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: My next question was: Did you give any newspaper interviews?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. On the 21st of November, 2007, I gave a long interview under my full name and surname. As a matter of fact, I disclosed my identity, and I informed the Serbian public about all the pressures that were exerted against me by the Office of the Prosecutor from The Hague and Zoran Djindjic, of course, from 2003 -- or, rather, from 2001 until 2007, or, rather, as I said, all the way up until the 27th of February, 2008.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: I'm afraid members of the Trial Chamber may have missed this. Could you repeat this once again? When did you give this long newspaper interview, when you said all of that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: Was that a year before the book was published?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that interview took place before the book was published. Well, about a year, at least.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: In my book, was this interview of yours published, along with the statements?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: Did you read the whole book?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: In the case of other people who gave statements to my team, did you see that I also published their newspaper interviews?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED FALLS WELL
utterances.text: For example, your newspaper interview can be found on page 85, entitled "Pressures on Jovan Glamocanin," and it goes on for a full five pages. And that's a lengthy book; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Glamocanin. With this, I have concluded my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to bring to your attention, Mr. Kwon, that I used exactly 20 minutes to examine this witness. And I'm really taking very good care about court time, and that should be done in the same way by everyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. Yes, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you follow -- do you hear me, Mr. Glamocanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to show you two documents which have been marked as an exhibit in these proceedings. For the record, the first is Exhibit 55F, and the second is Exhibit 55G. And with the assistance of the Court Usher, I'd like to direct your attention to paragraphs near the beginning of both of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: I have to put my glasses on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Do you see, near the beginning of both of those documents, a reference to your name?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Do I have to say my name? Yes, I have read it, this part that you pointed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Both documents? Do you see your name referred to in both documents?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: And do you see other personal --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: It's correct. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Do you see other personal information about yourself referred to at the same location in both documents?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I can see my personal details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: And are those details accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, they are. It's correct that my name is Jovan Glamocanin, that I am a lawyer by profession, that I am a member of the Academy of Sciences, that I live in Pancevo, Veljka Vlahovica number 11, that I was born in Subotica, and that my ID card number is such and such, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any redirect examination, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Glamocanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I thank you for coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break of five minutes to prepare for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was advised that we don't need such preparatory time. Then I would like to invite you to call your next witness, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, the fact that we do not need any preparations, does that indicate that this witness is going to testify in public? Shall I call him by saying his full name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. He's given only a pseudonym, so we --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Therefore, I call the seventh Defence witness, marked by you as DS-3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Would the Prosecutor please switch off his microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness. How are you today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you begin your testimony, I would like to inform you that you will be called not by your name, but by a pseudonym, due to an existing court order of protective measures. So you'll be called today as "DS-3." Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something? Mr. Kwon, I believe that you should ask this witness if he wants to testify in public under his full name. This witness used to be on the Prosecution list, and the Prosecution, themselves, decided not to call him. The Prosecution office did not insist on his appearance in the main trial. Now, these protective measures, are they going to be imposed and in place when this witness is concerned for the rest of his life?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I stopped you, Mr. Seselj. If you wanted this witness to testify in public with his full name, you should have applied to that Chamber to lift that protective measure in advance. I think you know the Rule by now. Please start your examination, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, this witness had protective measures granted for him for as long as somebody in the main trial counted on his testimony. The moment he was removed from the Prosecution witness list, and when the Trial Chamber gave up on him, what kind of protective measures are still in place when this witness is concerned? I'm not going to examine him whilst the protective measures are being in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's not waste time anymore. So you are withdrawing this witness from your Defence -- from your list of witnesses; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is impossible for me to examine him as a Defence witness. He agreed to testify in public, without any protective measures. He gave a number of statements in that respect. He came here with the intention of doing so. However, if you insist on the protective measures, I am not going to examine this witness under pseudonym. You didn't even ask him if he wants to have protective measures or not. Does that mean that if somebody in the main trial introduced protective measures, they remain in place for eternity? The Trial Chamber and the Prosecution have already forgotten all of this, and I'm not going to write any applications to them, and you cannot make me do so. And this witness, if I give up on his testimony, once he leaves this courtroom, he's going to talk to the media, and he will tell them what happened in this courtroom. Is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's better for him to testify in this courtroom, rather than in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Judge's microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I take your submission to be withdrawing this witness from your witness list. The Chamber does not see any point of continuing the proceedings with this witness, then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that is your conclusion, that's up to you, but I am not going to examine any Defence witness under protective measures. I am preparing witnesses for the main trial, and I am going to call all of them to come here and testify in public. Otherwise, they will not testify at all, because there is a principle of public testimony. Only people who have no clear conscience insist on private testimony, and amongst my witnesses there is not a single person who doesn't have a clear conscience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, while I find this development to be very unfortunate, I would like to thank you for your coming all the way to The Hague to co-operate with this Tribunal. As you observed, since Mr. Seselj withdrew you from his witness list, there is no further point of keeping you here. Now you are free to go. Thank you very much, again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I want to check with you whether your position is the same with the upcoming witnesses, Witnesses number 8, 9 and 10; i.e., you're not minded --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not minded to call them unless the protective measures are not lifted -- unless the protective measures are lifted?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, the eighth witness, whom you marked as "DS-4," also did not appear in the main trial. The Prosecution kept him on the list for a certain period of time, and then they removed him from the list, themselves. And Witness number 10, marked by you as "DS-6," the same applies to him. Only Witness number 9 appeared in the main trial, and he expressed his wish to testify here in public. So number 8 and number 9 never appeared in the main trial. Somebody put them on the Prosecution list. The Trial Chamber introduced blanket protective measures without going into any specifics, and then suddenly the Prosecution decided to give up on protective measures in the case of these two. So what does that mean? The protective measures do not exist anymore. The moment the Prosecution gave up on them, it was all finished. You can try and interpret this any way you like, but that is how things stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, it strikes me that all of the things that you've said are likely to be a strong basis for a successful application to the Trial Chamber that made the protective measures to withdraw them, as a matter of law and as a matter of logic. Wouldn't it cut the Gordian knot, simply, to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. Morrison. I have no reason to think ill of you. I think that your intentions are good. My goal is not to cut the Gordian knot, but rather to get it entangled even more. That's my right, and nobody can deny that right. These witnesses that the Prosecution had planned initially for them to appear in the main trial, and then gave up on them, I immediately accepted as Defence witnesses. The ongoing proceedings has to do -- at least some connection with the main trial, in the sense that an accused cannot be tried for contempt of court. He can be punished by an on-the-spot punishment; to be thrown out of the courtroom, to have his microphone turned off, et cetera. Mr. Morrison, I'm fully aware that you come from the legal system that it is impossible for contempt of court proceedings to be conducted against an accused. This is something that was made up here, because they cannot find any other way of dealing with me. And I am not backing off an inch, because I decided, if necessary, let's have 10 contempt of court proceedings. This is the second one, the third one has already been announced, and we have another seven coming up in the future. I want to demonstrate to you here that things are being done here that have no foundation in either system, Anglo-Saxon or the Continental one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I think you can take it from me -- I hope you can take it from me, Mr. Seselj, that you can, in fact, bring contempt of court proceedings in the common-law system, although I agree it's very rarely done, and only in extreme circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to confirm with you, finally, that you are not minded to examine the remaining three witnesses with protective measures.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to respond to Judge Morrison. It is true that in the Anglo-Saxon legal system, there is a notion of criminal liability for contempt of court, but please cite at least a single case that this was conducted against an accused. You can do that if somebody is exerting pressure on witnesses, or trying to intimidate witnesses, et cetera, but do you know of any single case that court contempt proceedings were conducted against a defendant who had already been accused and charged with the most serious crime? I don't think that that exists in your jurisprudence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, tempting though it is to engage in a legal debate, we don't have the time for it, Mr. Seselj. The sort of proceedings you anticipate against someone who interferes with the course of justice are normally charged as an attempt to pervert the course of justice, for instance, witness interference, but individual accused can be indicted or summarily dealt with for contempt of court in certain circumstances. But I have to say, in 40-odd years in Great Britain, I never have personally had to deal with it, although I know others that have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Morrison, let's look at these specific circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to continue this debate in my closing argument. This is going to be one of the subjects of my closing argument. You cannot prevent me from doing so. But apparently we have finished with the witnesses, because you're not allowing me to call the remaining three witnesses whilst the protective measures are in force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then I take it that you rested your case. I take it there is no -- I'll leave it. Just I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, although the Presiding Judge has asked this question, I'm not sure that we got a direct answer from you, you have elected to not examine the remaining witnesses, for the reasons you indicated. That is your case, is it, in terms of calling witnesses? We appreciate that you have a right to make a closing statement, but moving along procedurally, we just want it clear for the record that you have no more witnesses to call and that is the end of your case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and that was due to the fact that the acts of the Trial Chamber were unlawful. You unlawfully prevented me from examining these witnesses. The witnesses wanted to testify in public, I wanted to question them in public. However, you invoked protective measures introduced in a completely different proceedings, irrespective of these proceedings, because what the witnesses are testifying here about is nothing to do with what is going to be discussed in the main trial. The only thing that the witnesses are speaking about here are -- is how it happened that their statements were published in my book. This is the crux of the matter and the essence of these proceedings, and the only issue here is to establish whether this was done with or without their consent. I think that is the essence of their giving evidence. And I'm honestly telling you that in the main trial, I'm not going to accept any witnesses under protective measures. More than half of the witnesses who have appeared were under the protective measures, which constitutes a brutal violation of the rights of the accused. Everybody must see how things are being conducted here. We might have a situation that somebody can come here, give a false testimony, people will recognise that, and then I will have at least a dozen people coming back to me, saying, We have different evidence to provide. Judges, you are being judged by the public. You are judging me, but you are being judged by the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder, Mr. MacFarlane, whether you are prepared to proceed with the closing argument today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes, I am prepared to proceed. I would appreciate a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much would you need to prepare? About half an hour would be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And how long -- can I ask how long it will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I expect it will be approximately an hour. Maybe just a few minutes more than that, but around an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Seselj, I wonder whether you also are -- you are also prepared to proceed with your closing argument today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am ready for my closing argument, and my closing argument will definitely not be shorter than Mr. MacFarlane's. If you allocate one hour to him, I expect you to give me also one hour. And I also insist on another thing as well. If Mr. MacFarlane wants to take the floor after my closing argument, I request to have the right to rejoinder, because in every proceedings it is the accused who is entitled to have the last say with respect to the Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 20 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As I mentioned earlier, I expect I will be -- we will be an hour. I propose to, in my initial comments that should run for a little bit more than half an hour, to address the evidence that you've heard. The Chamber will remember that there's two parts to this case. One is a hard-copy book aspect, and then there's also an electronic aspect to this, and my colleague, Ms. Wanlin, will deal with that, after which, for probably no more than three or four minutes, I will do a wrap-up with a recommendation. I should also say, by way of preliminary comment, that some of the detail -- a considerable amount of detail, in terms of the evidence, is set out in the pre-trial brief that we filed before the trial. I've reviewed that, and not much has changed in terms of the case for the Prosecution, so that I would urge the Chamber to take a look at the pre-trial brief because it provides a level of detail that I don't propose to go through in my oral comments now. It's my hope that I will be able to, in my portions of the closing address, to continue in open session. It's difficult to do that in a publication contempt case, because, of necessity, you're talking about the breaches or alleged breaches of protective measures, but I've endeavoured to tailor my comments in a more general way so the Chamber can follow the general tenor of the case for the Prosecution without getting into some of the sensitive areas. That is how I propose to proceed this afternoon. I'd open by a brief comment on Rule 77, noting that it provides that: "The Tribunal, in the exercise of its inherent power, may hold in contempt those who disclose information, in knowing violation of an order of the Chamber." On the facts in this case, I would like to comment on the rationale underlying this provision. In the context of a publication contempt, the danger or the harm sought to be avoided has many different faces. In some cases, it involves witnesses who are very frightened. In other cases, as I'll be pointing out, it can involve individuals who, over the passage of time, have had their concerns diminish somewhat. But the rationale, as I'll be pointing to probably at the end of my submission, the rationale under this -- in the context of this type of case, is that it is not up to an individual party or an individual witness to say, Oh, I want to have protective measures, or, Oh, I don't want to. The process at both ends, that is, at the commencement of the process and at the end, is controlled by the Chamber for good reason; so there is a judicial filtering of whether either is appropriate, that is, whether it's appropriate to have protective measures, because there needs to be evidence, and, correspondingly, whether it is appropriate to terminate or rescind those protective measures. That is clear, and there's good reason for that. That's not just an arbitrary Rule. If that wasn't in place, if there was no judicial filter or control, that could actually end up placing witnesses in more danger because there would be, on the part of some people, to attempt to intimidate them into having their protective measures lifted. That is the role of the Chamber, is to ensure that that sort of intimidation does not take place, and, therefore, it needs to be filtered at both ends. The core elements in the case have been the subject of some discussion between the parties and the Chamber. It's my submission that there are four core elements in this case: First of all, were there protective measures in place; secondly, who was protected; thirdly, did the accused objectively breach the protective measures in his book; and, finally, was it deliberate, that is, was the breach deliberate, or was it an accident. And the Chamber will recall, at the beginning of the proceedings when there was a discussion on what the case was all about and the scope of the case, the Presiding Judge, Judge Kwon, said this: "As I indicated, Mr. MacFarlane, the Chamber is of the view to limit the scope of this case to the sole issue, whether he violated the order of the Court by publishing that book in the way of revealing the identity and the protected statements of those protected witnesses." That's at page 70, lines 20 to 24. And that's still, in my respectful submission, the case at the end of the proceedings. The facts in the case are relatively straightforward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are hearing French. Could you repeat, Mr. MacFarlane, from "the facts in the case." I think it's been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: The facts in this case are relatively straightforward. And as I mentioned earlier, I'll endeavour to paint the evidence and describe the contours of the evidence in a fairly general way so that I'm not moving from public to private. But the foundation of the case rests on several orders of Chambers that were obtained over a period of time. The first two were all-embracing and non-specific to individual witnesses, and I'm referring to Exhibits 23 and 24. The first one focused on the confidentiality of disclosure, and the second focused again on confidentiality of disclosure materials. So that was the starting point for the case. Subsequently, the Trial Chamber ordered various protective measures that were specific to the 11 witnesses named in the order in lieu of indictment, and those orders were issued on the 1st of June, 2005 - that's Exhibit 25 - August 30th, 2007 - Exhibit 27 - and October 16, 2007 - Exhibit 29. Dealing with the first of those specific orders, and I intend to be as general as I can, under Exhibit 25, the Trial Chamber was unanimous in granting protective measures. And it is important to note that the order was issued on the basis of evidence, specific evidence that was before the Chamber, and the orders were tailored to the individuals to be protected and the evidence that was adduced. Pseudonyms were assigned on the basis of the evidence that was provided, but there was a consideration of specific evidence. The second was issued and is in tab 27 -- Exhibit 27. This was before the Pre-Trial Judge, and it gave a very detailed set of protective measures involving individual assessments of whether there should be, simply, pseudonyms until they give evidence. There were 22 such witnesses. Ten of them are named in the order in lieu of indictment in this case. In some instances, there was the assignment of a pseudonym for use throughout the duration of the current proceedings. There are 36 such witnesses. And in some instances, delayed disclosure was authorised, image distortion -- image and voice distortion, and proceeding in closed session. Once again, there were very clear distinctions made between the witnesses, based on a tailoring arising from the evidence provided to the Chamber. The third specific order was before the Pre-Trial Judge again, concerning 19 witnesses. Some of those applications were, in fact, refused. Some were granted, and two are relevant to these proceedings, involving VS-014 and VS-032. Once again, the point is that there was a very careful consideration of the evidence, based on what had been presented to the Chamber. So the position that the Tribunal and the Chamber found itself in, in late 2007, was that specific protective measures were in place for all 11 of our protected witnesses. The evidence during the course of the trial demonstrated that, through proces-verbal and submissions from the accused, that he knew that the protective measures were in place and he knew that pseudonyms had been assigned. Of that, there can be no doubt. He signed the proces-verbal, and we have submissions, which have been tendered in evidence, demonstrating his knowledge of the existence of the protective measures and the witnesses that were affected. The evidence also demonstrates that the accused was aware of the fact that there was a prohibition against publishing the statements of protected witnesses, and that he knew he had to go to the Chamber to have protective measure orders rescinded or varied. I've made reference to some of those decisions during the course of my submissions in the trial today, and they are included as exhibits in the Bar Table motion and before the Chamber. So there is no doubt that the accused knew that the protective measures were in place and that the Chamber controlled the process. That is critical, in my respectful submission, in terms of the issues in this case. By late 2007 and mid 2008, in other words, prior to the publication of the book in question, which I'll, for purposes of my submission, I'll simply refer to as the 2008 book, during that late 2007 to mid 2008 period, you've seen in the exhibits before you a fair bit of evidence, not only demonstrating an understanding of the protected witness framework in the Rules on the part of the accused, but that during that period, he became quite litigious on the question of protective measures and witnesses. His submissions detail the Rules and detail the control exercised by the Chamber. And, in fact, with respect to one aspect of his motions, where he had been unsuccessful, he proceeded to the Appeals Chamber and continued to litigate the issue. Through his submissions and the decisions that resulted, it is quite evidence, in my submission, that the accused had actual knowledge that the Chamber controlled the process, that the Chamber only could rescind or vary, and, in fact, with respect to one witness, the accused actually insisted on seeking a variation through a formal application to the Chamber. And further than that, the accused actually brought a Defence request for protective measures just before the book emerged. His steps that followed in the book, in my respectful submission, there is no other inference that can be drawn or conclusion that can be reached but that the breaches were done knowingly, they were deliberate, and, in my respectful submission, the evidence can only be interpreted as that his position was one of defiance towards the Chamber. And that's exactly what the contempt powers were intended to deal with. If one was to fast-forward a bit to the fall of 2008, I won't refer to the specific date, but the evidence before you demonstrates that the 2008 book came out in the fall of that year. And, in fact, the evidence is much more specific than that. It virtually pin-points a date. The evidence before you, in terms of the transcripts that have been tendered - some are in private session, some are in open - the transcripts demonstrate that the accused is the author of the 2008 book. And on the basis of the evidence as a whole, there doesn't appear to be any dispute on that; that appears to be common ground, although there was no formal admission in that respect. The timing of the publication of the book is clear, in the way that I've just described it, and the orders were all in place at the time of publication, subject to VS-010, where the pseudonym was lifted, but the rest of the protective measures remained in place. It would be open to the Chamber to conclude that by virtue of the litigation in which the accused engaged unsuccessfully with respect to protective measures, in some fashion prompted the publication of the book because, on the one hand, you have a clear understanding of the role of the Chamber, and then later that same year, you have the situation where the book starts to roll out in both hard copy and electronic. The book breached the orders in two respects. First of all, it disclosed information that enabled the reader to identify the 11 protected witnesses by publishing their full names, publishing their address, publishing their identity card numbers. And you heard the witnesses look at it and say, Yeah, that's me, that's my personal information. And in several instances, the book went further than that to include identifying information such as date of birth, place of birth, occupation, and unique citizen numbers. This is not a case where the identifying information tends to, or is capable, or may identify a protected witness. This is a case where the information published actually does identify the protected witness. The 2008 book goes, actually, further than that. In addition to focusing on identifying information, there is a second aspect to the breaches, and that is the book reprints witness statements from submissions to the Chamber that had been reclassified by Chambers as confidential. So there's really two dimensions to the breaches, the information and the submissions that the accused had filed, which have been reclassified to his knowledge. And you have proces-verbal in the evidence, and you also have the filing policy which was delivered to him as evidence by proces-verbal. So there can be no doubt that there was two aspects, and two aspects to his knowledge. The submissions clearly originated from the accused, were reclassified, and invariably, on the face of the first page, it is noted that it was reclassified at the direction of the Chamber. So there was formal notice to the accused that these were confidential and could not be published, but they were. Concerning the evidence as a whole and the 2008 book, it's my submission that the evidence has demonstrated beyond a reasonable doubt that the publication of the information was deliberate and defiant, and certainly not accidental. The accused knew about the orders and decided to publish identifying information in any event. That's a quick overview of the case for the Prosecution. I would like to provide the Chamber with my submissions concerning the evidence adduced by the accused. I think it's fair to say that certainly with respect to the first two or three witnesses, we were all over the map, and almost all of the evidence was not relevant to the issues as I identified them at the beginning of my comments. So my overall submission is that the vast majority of the evidence tendered by the accused is not responsive to the true issues in the case and, for that reason, is largely irrelevant. Perhaps the high-water mark for the case for the Defence was evidence concerning some of the witnesses, who indicated that now they didn't mind if the evidence was published. That's now and in recent times. The law on that is quite clear. The Jovic decision from the Appeals Chamber is, in my view, in my respectful submission, virtually dispositive on this point. The Appeals Chamber said: "An order remains in force until a Chamber decides otherwise. The fact that some portions of the witness's written statement or closed-session testimony may have been disclosed by another third party does not mean that this information was no longer protected, that the court order had been, de facto, lifted, or that its violation would not interfere with the Tribunal's administration of justice." To a like effect and to take the matter even further, the Appeals Chamber delivered a decision in Marijacic and Rebic. In that particular case, significantly, the protective measures granted to the witness were lifted after he had testified, but before charges were laid. The accused was, nonetheless, found guilty at trial, and the conviction was affirmed on appeal, with the Appeals Chamber saying as follows: "A court order remains in force until a Chamber decides otherwise. The Appeals Chamber, proprio motu, notes that the fact that the aforementioned information today is no longer confidential does not present an obstacle to a conviction for having published the information at a time when it was still under protection." Those two decisions, in my submission, are virtually dispositive of this case. I will, in my closing comments, have some remarks with respect to the seriousness of the breach, as well as a recommendation with respect to the sentence that would seem to be appropriate in the event of conviction. But before I deal with that, and I'll deal with that in a matter of perhaps four or five minutes, I would like to turn to my colleague for a submission with respect to the electronic side of the case, if I can call it that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WANLIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. In the event of a finding of guilt, the scope of the disclosure is a factor that should be considered for sentencing. And if I might, I would like to move into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Ms. Wanlin.

utterances.speaker: MS. WANLIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The availability of the book in electronic format on the accused's web site is a fundamentally different nature than his hard-copy version. The fact that the web site is his own, and that he controls the content on the web site, has been established in several documents, including P8 through 13 and P14 through 17, as well as others. I don't believe that issue is in dispute, but it's good to establish for the record. The fact that the book has been published on-line can be seen through Exhibits P58.1 and 59, which are both screenshots of the publication in question. The date of the publication on-line, although we can't establish it directly, we can note that it is through the Exhibits P63 and P64, that these are references to the book on a web forum. And if you look at the arrows on those respective exhibits, you will note that there are dates that those entries have been made. So other individuals have made reference to the fact that this book has been published on the accused's web site. I won't mention the dates, but they are identified quite clearly on the exhibits. The fact that the book remains on-line has been made clear through the submissions of the accused at the last hearing on the 22nd of February of this year, as well as we have a submission from December of this year that sets the date there as well. By making the book available in PDF format on his web site, the accused is able to accomplish a number of things that he could not do in the print format. I would turn your attention to P57.1, which it states on the web site that it is available in PDF format and that it can be downloaded free of charge. This ensures that he has unlimited and immediate access to his existing readership. Readers don't have to go to a bookstore, they don't have to order anything to be delivered. In the matter of a few keystrokes, they can have the information that they are seeking. He's not bound by costs associated with publication. He has an unlimited number. The second factor I would like to point out is that this web site is indexed. And if you'll allow me to explain the importance of this fact. It allows the accused to increase his readership. An individual who might not know about the book, but is interested in the proceedings, might hear a name, enter it into a search engine, and a number of entries come up, including the book of the accused. And, therefore, someone who might not necessarily know to look through a book that is several hundreds of pages has found it again in a matter of a few clicks of a mouse and a few keystrokes. Typically, materials and information can be hidden in a book, and when you pick up a book, you don't necessarily know which words are found in it or which names, as is relevant in this circumstance. I would draw your attention to P60, P61 and P62 for support for that premise. What you will see in these exhibits is a key-word search of the -- sorry, I'm referring to P60 at the moment. It's in Cyrillic, the names of certain of the individuals who have been identified by the book. And you'll note in each of these references that this is on the very first page of a Google search. And for any of you who have done a key-word search, the first hits are the ones that you usually will refer to. So this is not hidden in the obscurity of pages and pages down. This is the first hits that come up. Another factor that I would like to point out is: Because the book is available in PDF format, the reader doesn't have to sift through pages and pages and pages to find what they're looking for. If they hear a name being referred to in gossip or chatter at the cafe, they can simply go to the PDF document, enter it in, and in a matter of seconds they have found the information that they're looking for, unlike having to go through a book of a hundred -- or several hundred pages, pardon me. Therefore, finding the information, whether by accident or with intent, is much easier through the electronic disclosure than it would be in the hard-copy disclosure. The next factor that should be considered is that once the accused made this information available on his web site, individuals who are interested might, as we have seen through the evidence, make a link on another web site. And you'll note that Exhibits P63 and P67 are examples of different web forums where individuals have posted links to Mr. Seselj's web site, and specifically links to the book, in particular. An individual who goes to that forum simply has to click on that link and the book is available immediately. Now, it's not simply these web forums, that might be somewhat obscure, that refer to this book, but a quite well-known web site, Wikipedia, I think that average users that might not have any interest in the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, the matters that we are dealing with on a regular basis here in The Hague, might go to Wikipedia and come across a link to this web site -- pardon me, to the book, specifically, which adds a certain degree of credibility to the source. You can find the references to that in Exhibit P68. I will also point out that the URL for these last sections go directly back to the web site of the accused. Therefore, removing the book from the web site will effectively eliminate the fact that references can be made back through these hyperlinks. However, I would turn your attention to Exhibit P70, which is another phenomena that results from electronic publication, and that is: Once a document is made available, other sites might host it. So after the accused made his book available on his web site, somebody who has one of these file-sharing web sites simply can take a copy of the book and uploads it on their site. If you notice Exhibit P71, what is happening in that exhibit, somebody has clicked the link and it opens up the book. The challenge that is faced by those wanting to reduce the scope of the publication is that even removing the book from the web site at this point will have no affect on those. The evidence has two different sites that are currently hosting the book. Therefore, my submission is that the scope of the disclosure is significantly increased as a result of publication on-line. Now, a second factor that should be considered is a fact that was mentioned in the last hearing, and that is that the accused has endeavoured to stay in front of the actions of the Registry to remove the publications. He has moved his web site from place to place to place, from web host to web host to web host, which suggests a defiance that needs to be considered as an aggravating circumstance in this case. And I will turn the microphone over to my colleague, Mr. MacFarlane. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: It appears that I will be able to complete within -- well within the one-hour period, happily. I'll just take, perhaps, four or five minutes to deal with the issue of aggravating circumstances, because I do submit that that plays an important role in this case. The actions of the accused, I submit, can be summarised with three descriptors, three words. His actions were deliberate, his actions were disingenuous, and his actions were defiant. And I would like to point to half a dozen aspects of the case in support for that proposition. Number 1, the publications emerged after quite full and vigorous litigation conducted by the accused. Number 2, the Chamber afforded the accused an opportunity to remove the book from the web site through a qualified order, give him a chance to deal with it, and he didn't. An unqualified order resulted to remove the book from his web site. The evidence also demonstrates that in terms of the electronic side of the case, that the accused has engaged at least one relative to assist him, and I submit that that is an aggravating feature of the case. In Exhibit 4 of the Bar Table motion evidence that was tendered in open session, the Presiding Judge in the main trial gave the accused a very specific warning about not publishing protected witnesses. He did that on the 3rd of April of 2008, several months before publication. The Presiding Judge said: "As you know, Mr. Seselj, you're a qualified lawyer, so you know, like everyone here, the statements of protected witnesses are, by definition, also protected, and it's absolutely banned to publish, outside this legal arena, these kinds of comments." The Presiding Judge also said that the consequences could be huge for failing to abide by the law. So we have a warning specifically on the record and public. The accused's position overall, his broad position, in my respectful submission, is quite disingenuous. He appears to say that if a witness or he doesn't see a need for confidentiality, that they're really not protected witnesses. Tab 5 -- Exhibit 5 is instructive in that respect. It was in private session, so I will simply note the page number so that it can be noted. It's page 10995. And in tab 11, a similar demonstration by the accused that he's really the one that's going to make the assessment of confidentiality. It's in private session, so I'll simply note the page number, which is page 5831. My colleague, Ms. Wanlin, alluded to a further aggravating feature, but I'd like to take it a bit further. The accused noted that -- in open session that he had sold 10.000 of the hard-copy books, but, significantly, he then moved it onto the web site. So it was a compounding of the contemptuous act. His reference to the 10.000 copies can be found in Exhibit 5. The accused, in the next feature -- the second-last feature that I'd like to comment on, seemed to be almost flippant in terms of removing the book from the web site. His view was that, Well, we'll wait until the proceedings are completed, and then I'll see. It's Exhibit 16, page 14749, lines 15 and 16. And, finally, with a touch of irony, the accused appears to believe that with being charged with contempt, that actually increases interest in his book, increases interest in his web site, and so, in a bizarre sense, he almost appears to be welcoming being charged because it advances his agenda; in open session, Exhibit 14. Given those aggravating circumstances, and given the fact of a previous conviction for contempt of court, which is before the Court - it's a matter of public record - for which he was sentenced to 15 months, it's my respectful submission that in the event of a conviction on this occasion, the appropriate sentence would be in the vicinity of three years' imprisonment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for 15 minutes and then hear from you, Mr. Seselj. We resume at 25 past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Hague Tribunal is an illegal court. That court was established by an organ of the United Nations, the Security Council. That is, indeed, a high organ of the United Nations, but according to the Charter, this organ does not have the right to establish international courts of law. Therefore, the Security Council abused Chapter 7 of the Charter that speaks of measures to be taken in order to establish peace anywhere in the world. And as one of the peacekeeping measures, they claim that the ad hoc tribunal of the former Yugoslavia could be one. Normal courts of law have the right to administer justice, to establish justice, not peace. Justice and peace are two very different interests.
